Certainly could do, but why invent new phrasings when we already have
a perfectly good set in they/their/them? And what would be the xe
equivalents for him/her and his/hers? Xim? Xirs?

The whole 'yo' thing seems to be more a laziness in speech than
anything, collapsing anything not I or me into one word, as I'm sure
the yo developed from the more common use of 'yo' for 'you' and
'your'. Worse still, the new use of 'yo' encompasses he/she, him/her
and likely his/hers as well.

Having to make a choice, I'd prefer the Xe hierarchy, as it at least
bears some resemblence to the he/she predecessors. Yo would just be
more confusing than not, as your mind would have to do a double think
to differentiate from 'you' or 'he/she', especially when spoken, as we
tend to speak fairly ungrammatically.

"Yo speak to Bob lately?"

"Yeah, yo is doin' fine."

"Cool. Haven't spoken to yo in a while. Hey, yo goin' to the game
tonight?"

Even in context with both speakers, it's not clear at all just who
'yo' is in the last quote. Is it Bob, or is it the other speaker? Even
if we 'fixed' the last quote grammatically, the first yo would still
be ambiguous. "Cool. I haven't spoken to yo in a while. Hey, are yo
going to the game tonight?"

Oh well, the dark times of English Gehenna are nigh!

Chris, Thrall of Arika

Maybe. But sometimes dictionaries don't reflect the intuitive
sensibilities of the population. It's a gray area, certainly. But
there's a reason languages evolve over time. Dictionaries have no
inherent claim to correctness other than the judgment of the particular
author who, hopefully, reflects the prevalent condition in society.

change. So maybe I erred when I told Kevin I thought "most people" don't
consider "he" to be correct to use for a person of unspecified sex.

word that also applies to one particular sex probably strikes a lot
of people as inaccuate when they use it to refer to a person of
unspecified sex. And whether dictionaries agree or not is ultimately
beside the point.

Shouldn't he and she be spelt "hee" and "shee"? Why isn't tough spelt
tuff? There are many, many words we can go on about spelling versus
pronounciation. Also, the assertion that mispronounciations will occur
due to foreign cultures is self-evident, we do it enough as it is with
the borrowed words used in VTES. Is it bru-hah, or bru-jah (original
word derived from Spanish)? Sam-di or sa-mee-di (original word derived
from French)? I hear both versions on a regular occasion.

But considering that xe is not borrowed from another culture, there is
no impetus to borrow pronunciations from other cultures. And really,
if any mispronunciation is to occur, it would be making it a 'hard' x,
due to the popularity of turning ex- words into x- words (xtreme, for
example). Personally, I've pronounced is 'zee' from the first I saw
it, since that seems follow best from he/she pronunciations, which the
word is attempting to replace, and virtually all normal x words have a
soft zed sound.

Yo may be easier to look at and pronounce, but I've already shown that
it can be far to ambiguous. One thing that can't be overlooked is that
the development of new terms cannot take place in a vacuum. Yo already
has a foothold in the pronoun game, it seems silly to accept it for
replacing yet more pronouns, when it seems the desire is to get away
from already existing terms that are too encompassing (they/their/
them).

If xe is to take hold, the pronounciation would follow as it entered
verbal vocabulary. The difficulty is that it's main use now is in
writing to replace the cumbersome he/she or s/he text. So no
pronunciation is evident, since it's a new word, and we haven't grown
up with it or have much use of it orally.

Chris, Thrall of Arika

1) It is OK, gramatically, to use "he" as a third-person singular pronoun
when referring to a person of non-specific gender.

2) But, because "he" is ALSO used as a third-person singular pronoun when
referring to a person of strictly male gender, it is therefore ambiguous.

comments they can be confident are understood correctly by the readers.

correctness, per se. Granted, excess sensitivity to the issue may have
its roots in political correctness but since you can't read minds,
making such an accusation on that basis alone is inherently baseless.

desire to use a more streamlined alternative is not, AFAICS, politically
correct either.

I just had to reply to this. In Finnish spoken language (at least
where I live in south west) this is how it goes. We have a very good
3rd person singular pronoun "hän" (engl. "he/she/it"), but in the
local spoken language it's gotten a kind of derogatory meaning.
Usually when we use it, we are making a between the lines remark that
the person we are speaking about thinks that he's more important than
he really is. Instead of the 3rd person pronoun we use the 3rd
demonstrative pronoun "se" (engl. "it/that") when speaking without
between the lines meanings. So... if you english speaking think that
using a pronoun normally used for inhumane things is derogatory, we
finns think that using a pronoun normally used for humans derogatory :)

Oh, man, I really see that issue differently. The thing is, I really
don't like the concept of salting a set of low-demand cards with a few
VERY high-demand cards to create sales. Every time this has been tried,
it's caused problems. As I alluded to in my prior post, in practise it
has the effect of "super-rarizing" the rare cards. That is, the high
demand cards become even rarer because the overall demand for the set
is low - so sales are low, so the actual number of rare cards in
circulation because VERY low. In the case of 3E, the set having most
all reprint library cards means that older players have much less
reason to buy it except for the tiny handful of new library cards and
the vampires. The same thing happened in Camarilla Edition. What was
the result? To alleviate customer demand in the end, White Wolf had to
make a special project of reprinting all the vampires by themselves in
their own special single box. Will 3E be the same a few years down the
road? I wouldn't be surprised. In fact, I can't see any reason why
it won't.

Fortunately, the were no super-useful rare cards among the non-reprint
library cards in CE. No one really missed out on Brothers Grimm or
Abandoning the Flesh. Some of them, like Gregory Winter and Tension in
the Ranks were useful, but nothing like on the order of HoN. Even
these don't really please me but the game didn't seem to suffer
appreciably. I think it does when a truly useful card is excessively
hard to get.
